# Russia Weighs Escalated Missile Strikes; Black Sea Grain Supply Fears Send Wheat Limit-Up to 3-Year High

[Add to Google Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com)

1

All three major agricultural futures on the Chicago Board of Trade rallied on August 26 as escalating Russia-Ukraine hostilities reignited fears of Black Sea grain supply disruptions. Wheat futures surged limit-up to their highest level in more than three years, settling at $7.4825 per bushel. Corn and soybean contracts across all delivery months touched contract lifecycle highs, closing at $5.365 and $12.66 per bushel, respectively. Separately, the European Union's tariff-free import quota for Ukrainian wheat has been exhausted, diverting Ukrainian export flows toward Danube River ports and Romania's Port of Constanta, where logistics bottlenecks are creating hidden costs. Market participants noted that China's absence from the latest U.S. sanctions list bodes well for continued Chinese purchases of American soybeans.

# Chips & tokens at the fault lines: Two stacks in one fragmenting world

SUERF Policy Note | No. 416 | 27 Aug, 2026

## Author(s):

## Keywords:

## Download:

 [SUERF Policy Note, No 416](https://www.suerf.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SUERF-Policy-Note-416_-Natalucci-Rebucci.pdf)

This policy brief is based on [Andersen Institute White Paper No. 01-2026](https://anderseninstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/AI-WP-02-2026.pdf). The views expressed are those of the authors and not necessarily those of the institutions the authors are affiliated with.

**Abstract**  
 The United States and China have each built the capacity to inflict serious economic damage on each other, and neither has used it in full. This brief argues that the resulting mutual vulnerability, the Cold War logic of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) now constrains both sides and prevents further decoupling. The brief maps this contest across two stacks: the real economy stack of computing, semiconductors and rare earths (economic MAD, or EMAD) and the financial stack of dollar dominance and digital finance (financial MAD, or FMAD). Implications for corporate leaders, markets and policy makers are also discussed.
